ru: идти (о дожде со снегом), сыпать ледяной крупой
gloss: To fall as a mix of rain and partly frozen snow.
examples: It usually *sleets* here for a day before it turns to real snow.
It *sleeted* the whole way to Chicago.
By noon it was *sleeting* hard and the roads were glazing over.
contrast: Like *rain* and *snow*, it takes the empty subject *it*: *It is sleeting*, never *The sky sleets*.

transitivity: both — transitive (ash *showered* the rooftops), intransitive (it *showered* twice)
gloss: To rain briefly, or to fall on something in a thick scatter.
examples: In Florida it *showers* nearly every afternoon in the summer.
It *showered* twice while we were driving home.
Ash was still *showering* the rooftops a day after the eruption.

transitivity: both — transitive (*mist* the plants), intransitive (the mirror *misted*)
gloss: To cover something with a fine spray of water, or to become covered with one.
examples: I *mist* the houseplants twice a week in winter.
The bathroom mirror *misted* the second she turned on the water.
A fine rain was *misting* the whole valley by noon.

gloss: To make the deep rolling noise that follows lightning, or a noise like it.
examples: When it *thunders*, the dog hides under the bed.
It *thundered* all night and nobody slept.
Trucks were *thundering* past the house every few minutes.
contrast: The weather sense takes the empty subject *it*: *It thundered for an hour*.

gloss: To fall in light, quick taps, the way rain does on a roof.
examples: Rain *patters* on the metal roof all through the fall.
Hail *pattered* against the windows for a minute and stopped.
We fell asleep to the sound of rain *pattering* on the tent.

gloss: To strike something again and again with rain, hail, or thrown objects.
examples: Hard rain *pelts* the west side of the house every winter.
Hail *pelted* the car so loudly that we had to pull over.
The kids were *pelting* each other with snowballs.

transitivity: both — transitive (rain *lashed* the windows), intransitive (waves *lashed* against the pier)
gloss: To hit something hard and repeatedly, the way wind-driven rain does.
examples: Winter storms *lash* this stretch of coast every year.
Rain *lashed* the windows until well after midnight.
Wind-driven rain was *lashing* the tents by the time we got back.
contrast: Ends in *-sh*, so the third-person form adds *-es*: *lashes*.

transitivity: both — transitive (waves *pound* the seawall), intransitive (the rain *pounded* down)
gloss: To hit something hard, heavily, and over and over.
examples: Surf *pounds* the seawall whenever a storm comes through.
Rain *pounded* the roof for three straight hours.
Waves were still *pounding* the beach a day after the hurricane.

gloss: To cover a whole area in an even layer of something.
examples: Fog *blankets* the bay almost every morning in June.
Six inches of snow *blanketed* the city overnight.
Ash from the fire was *blanketing* cars all over town.
contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, so the t is not doubled: *blanketed*, *blanketing* — compare *permit → permitted*.

gloss: To cover something completely so that it cannot be seen.
examples: Drifts *bury* the mailbox every January.
The avalanche *buried* two cabins on the lower slope.
Half the town is still *buried* under three feet of snow.
contrast: Spelled with a u but pronounced like *berry*: BER-ee. The y becomes ie in *buries* and *buried*, but stays in *burying*.

transitivity: both — transitive (steam *clouded* the mirror), intransitive (the sky *clouded*)
gloss: To fill or cover something with cloud, steam, or smoke so that it is hard to see through.
examples: Steam from the kettle *clouds* the window in seconds.
The sky *clouded* just after noon and the wind picked up.
Smoke from the wildfires has *clouded* the whole valley.

ru: заслонять, заслонить; скрывать, скрыть из виду
gloss: To block something from view or make it hard to see.
examples: Low clouds *obscure* the summit most mornings.
Smoke *obscured* the sun for a week.
The moon was already *obscuring* the edge of the sun when we looked up.

transitivity: both — transitive (the sun *dissipated* the fog), intransitive (the storm *dissipated*)
gloss: To break up and slowly disappear.
examples: Morning fog usually *dissipates* by ten o'clock.
The storm *dissipated* before it ever reached land.
The heat of the day was slowly *dissipating*.
contrast: Double s, single p: *dissipate*.

gloss: To appear large and threatening, especially close overhead or on the horizon.
examples: Thunderheads *loom* over the plains almost every July afternoon.
A wall of dust *loomed* on the horizon by four o'clock.
With a blizzard *looming*, the schools let out early.
contrast: Usually followed by *over* or *above*: *clouds loomed over the ridge*.

ru: готовиться, приготовиться (к удару стихии); укреплять, укрепить
transitivity: both — transitive (*brace* the shed), intransitive (they *braced* for the storm)
gloss: To get ready for something hard that is about to hit, or to make a structure stronger.
examples: Coastal towns *brace* for hurricanes every fall.
We *braced* the shed with two-by-fours before the wind hit.
The city is *bracing* for a foot of snow tonight.
contrast: Takes *for* in the sense of getting ready: *brace for a storm*.

gloss: To leave someone stuck in a place they cannot get out of.
examples: One good storm can *strand* hundreds of travelers at the airport.
The flood *stranded* twelve families on the north side of the river.
We were *stranded* in Denver for two days by the blizzard.

transitivity: both — transitive (the wind *slammed* the door), intransitive (the storm *slammed* into the coast)
gloss: To hit something with sudden violent force.
examples: When a nor'easter *slams* the coast, the ferries stop running.
The hurricane *slammed* into Louisiana just after midnight.
Wind was *slamming* the screen door all night.
contrast: One vowel plus one final consonant, so the m doubles: *slammed*, *slamming*.

gloss: To move fast and without stopping, especially toward something.
examples: Storms *barrel* across the plains from the west all spring.
The system *barreled* toward the coast at thirty miles an hour.
A semi came *barreling* down the icy hill behind us.
contrast: American English keeps one l: *barreled*, *barreling*; British English writes *barrelled*.

gloss: To blow in sudden short bursts of strong wind.
examples: The wind *gusts* hardest in the late afternoon.
It *gusted* to sixty miles an hour on the bridge.
Wind was *gusting* so hard the door pulled out of my hand.
contrast: Speeds take *to*: *the wind gusted to 60 miles an hour*.

gloss: To strike and shake something repeatedly, the way strong wind does.
examples: High winds *buffet* the bridge all winter long.
Turbulence *buffeted* the plane for twenty minutes.
Waves kept *buffeting* the little boat until it broke loose.
contrast: Not the same word as the *buffet* you eat at (buh-FAY): this verb is BUF-it.

gloss: To rise and roll outward in big soft masses, like smoke or a sail in the wind.
examples: Steam *billows* out of the vents on cold mornings.
Black smoke *billowed* over the ridge for hours.
The curtains were *billowing* in the wind off the lake.

transitivity: both — transitive (the breeze *wafted* the smell inside), intransitive (smoke *wafted* over the field)
gloss: To move gently through the air, or to carry something gently through it.
examples: The smell of woodsmoke *wafts* through the whole neighborhood in October.
Ash *wafted* down for hours after the fire.
A cool breeze was *wafting* off the lake.

gloss: To move in a curve that winds around a center, going up or down.
examples: Warm air *spirals* upward and gives the storm its shape.
A hawk *spiraled* over the field for ten minutes.
Smoke was *spiraling* out of the chimney into a still sky.
contrast: American English keeps one l: *spiraled*, *spiraling*; British English writes *spiralled*.

transitivity: both — transitive (the canyon *funnels* the wind), intransitive (cold air *funneled* down the valley)
gloss: To move through a narrow space, or to push something through one.
examples: The canyon *funnels* wind straight into town.
Rain *funneled* off the roof into the barrels.
Cold air was *funneling* down the valley all night.
contrast: American English keeps one l: *funneled*, *funneling*; British English writes *funnelled*.

gloss: To be the most common or the strongest thing in a place or a situation.
examples: Westerly winds *prevail* along this whole coast.
Clear skies *prevailed* right through the weekend.
The *prevailing* wind here comes straight off the ocean.
contrast: Takes *over* or *against* when it means to win: *reason prevailed over panic*.

gloss: To go on existing or happening for longer than expected.
examples: Drought conditions *persist* across most of the state.
The fog *persisted* until early afternoon.
With the heat wave *persisting*, the city opened cooling centers.
contrast: Takes *in* before a verb: *he persisted in walking home in the storm*.

gloss: To stay somewhere longer than you would expect, fading only slowly.
examples: Cold air *lingers* in the valley long after sunrise.
The smell of smoke *lingered* for days.
Snow was still *lingering* on the north slopes in June.

gloss: To become much less strong or less severe.
examples: Storms like this rarely *abate* before morning.
The wind *abated* right around dawn.
With the flooding finally *abating*, crews started clearing the roads.

ru: спадать, спасть; утихать, утихнуть; оседать (о почве)
gloss: To sink back down to a normal level, or to grow quiet again.
examples: Floodwaters usually *subside* within a day or two.
The shaking *subsided* after about thirty seconds.
Once the water had *subsided*, we could finally see the damage.

transitivity: both — transitive (cold *solidifies* the fat), intransitive (the lava *solidified*)
gloss: To become hard and solid, or to make something do that.
examples: Lava *solidifies* into black rock as soon as it hits the water.
The grease *solidified* in the cold pan overnight.
New land is *solidifying* where the flow reaches the sea.
contrast: The y becomes ie before -es and -ed: *solidifies*, *solidified*, but *solidifying*.

transitivity: both — transitive (heat *liquefies* the wax), intransitive (the soil *liquefied*)
gloss: To turn into liquid, or to turn something into liquid.
examples: Heat that intense *liquefies* the plastic siding.
The quake *liquefied* the wet soil under the houses.
The ice was *liquefying* faster than the drains could take it.
contrast: Spelled *liquefy*, not liquify — one of the most misspelled verbs in English.

transitivity: both — transitive (the heat *vaporized* the water), intransitive (the puddles *vaporized*)
gloss: To turn from liquid into gas, or to make something do that.
examples: Heat like that *vaporizes* standing water in minutes.
The puddles *vaporized* before the sun was even high.
Seawater is constantly *vaporizing* and falling again as rain.
contrast: American spelling *vaporize*; British English writes *vaporise*.

transitivity: both — transitive (the stove *radiates* heat), intransitive (cracks *radiated* from the center)
gloss: To send out heat or light in all directions, or to spread out from a center.
examples: Dark pavement *radiates* heat well into the night.
The stones *radiated* warmth long after the fire went out.
Cracks were *radiating* from the spot where the ice broke.

ru: изнывать от жары, страдать от зноя
gloss: To suffer from heat that is heavy and damp.
examples: The whole Midwest *swelters* through August.
We *sweltered* in the car until the air conditioning finally kicked in.
It was a *sweltering* afternoon with no breeze at all.

transitivity: both — transitive (the heat *dehydrates* you), intransitive (two hikers *dehydrated*)
gloss: To lose too much water from the body, or to dry something out completely.
examples: Dry mountain air *dehydrates* you faster than you think.
Two of the hikers *dehydrated* badly in the afternoon heat.
She was *dehydrating* apples for the winter.

ru: пить достаточно воды, восполнять запас влаги; увлажнять
transitivity: both — transitive (rain *hydrates* the soil), intransitive (*hydrate* before you hike)
gloss: To take in water, or to put water back into something dry.
examples: Start early and *hydrate* often in weather like this.
We *hydrated* all morning before starting up the ridge.
Staying *hydrated* matters most on hot, dry days.

transitivity: both — transitive (the sun *parched* the fields), intransitive (the ground *parches*)
gloss: To dry something out completely with heat.
examples: Weeks without rain *parch* the whole valley.
The sun *parched* the fields by early July.
The ground is *parched* and cracked right down to the fence line.
contrast: Ends in *-ch*, so the third-person form adds *-es*: *parches*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*acclimate* the plants slowly), intransitive (they *acclimated* fast)
gloss: To get used to a new climate or new conditions.
examples: It takes about a week to *acclimate* to this altitude.
They *acclimated* to the cold surprisingly fast.
We spent two days *acclimating* before the climb.
contrast: Takes *to*: *acclimate to the heat*. Americans say *acclimate*; the British usually say *acclimatize*.

ru: готовить к зиме, утеплять на зиму
gloss: To get a house, car, or boat ready to survive winter weather.
examples: We *winterize* the cabin every October.
They *winterized* the pipes a week before the hard freeze.
He is out back *winterizing* the boat.

transitivity: both — transitive (smoke *dims* the sun), intransitive (the light *dimmed*)
gloss: To become less bright, or to make something less bright.
examples: Smoke *dims* the sun for weeks during fire season.
The light *dimmed* as the eclipse reached its peak.
The sky was *dimming* fast and we still had a mile to go.
contrast: One vowel plus one final consonant, so the m doubles: *dimmed*, *dimming*.

transitivity: both — transitive (clouds *darkened* the room), intransitive (the sky *darkened*)
gloss: To become dark, or to make something dark.
examples: The sky *darkens* long before the rain actually arrives.
Clouds *darkened* the whole afternoon.
It was *darkening* in the west, so we packed up and left.

transitivity: both — transitive (sun *brightens* the room), intransitive (the sky *brightened*)
gloss: To become brighter or clearer, or to make something brighter.
examples: The sky usually *brightens* right after a summer storm.
The afternoon *brightened* once the fog burned off.
The horizon was *brightening* by five in the morning.

transitivity: both — transitive (*lighten* the pack), intransitive (the sky *lightened*)
gloss: To become lighter in color or in weight, or to make something lighter.
examples: The sky *lightens* around six this time of year.
The clouds *lightened* and the rain finally stopped.
The sky was just *lightening* when we set out.
contrast: *lightening* (getting lighter) is not *lightning* (the flash in a storm) — one letter apart.

gloss: To reach the highest point before going back down.
examples: The heat usually *peaks* around four in the afternoon.
The river *peaked* at twenty-two feet on Tuesday.
Temperatures have been *peaking* a little later every day.
contrast: *peak* (highest point) sounds exactly like *peek* (to look quickly) and *pique* (to annoy).

transitivity: both — transitive (cold *crystallizes* the honey), intransitive (frost *crystallized* on the glass)
gloss: To form crystals, or to make something form them.
examples: Frost *crystallizes* on the windows overnight.
The honey *crystallized* in the cold pantry.
Ice was *crystallizing* along the whole edge of the pond.
contrast: Double l even in American spelling: *crystallize*; British English writes *crystallise*.

gloss: To cover a place completely with water, or to overwhelm someone with too much of something.
examples: A high tide plus heavy rain *inundates* the low streets every fall.
The storm surge *inundated* the entire first block.
The county office has been *inundated* with calls about the flooding.

gloss: To flood a place with a huge amount of water, or with a huge amount of anything.
examples: One slow-moving storm can *deluge* the valley with a month of rain.
Rain *deluged* the coast for three days straight.
The station was *deluged* with calls after the levee failed.

gloss: To fill or cover something with water so that it cannot function.
examples: A wave like that can *swamp* a small boat in seconds.
The storm *swamped* dozens of basements on the east side.
We were *swamped* with water in about ten minutes.

transitivity: both — transitive (the river *submerged* the road), intransitive (the seal *submerged*)
gloss: To go under water, or to put something under water.
examples: Spring floods *submerge* the whole river road.
The water *submerged* two blocks of downtown.
The bridge was completely *submerged* by morning.

gloss: To soak something so completely that it cannot hold any more liquid.
examples: Two days of rain *saturate* the ground completely.
The storm *saturated* soil that was already soft.
With the hillside *saturated*, the county warned of slides.

gloss: To move back from a position it had reached.
examples: The tide *recedes* about a hundred yards along this beach.
The floodwater *receded* overnight and left a foot of mud.
The glacier has been *receding* for decades.

gloss: To flow back out, the way the tide does, or to grow slowly weaker.
examples: The tide *ebbs* twice a day here.
The water *ebbed* and left the boats sitting in the mud.
The storm's strength was already *ebbing* by sunrise.

ru: достигать высшей точки (о реке, волне); переваливать через гребень
transitivity: both — transitive (we *crested* the hill), intransitive (the river *crested*)
gloss: To reach the top or the highest level.
examples: The river usually *crests* two days after the rain stops.
The Mississippi *crested* at forty-four feet on Thursday.
A wave was *cresting* right over the seawall.

transitivity: both — transitive (water *breached* the levee), intransitive (the dike *breached*)
gloss: To break through a wall, a dam, or a barrier.
examples: A surge that high can *breach* the levee in an hour.
Floodwater *breached* the dike in two places.
The dam had already been *breached* when the sirens went off.
contrast: Ends in *-ch*, so the third-person form adds *-es*: *breaches*.

gloss: To flow out fast and in large amounts.
examples: Water *gushes* out of the culvert after every storm.
Mud *gushed* down the hillside and across the road.
A broken main was *gushing* into the street all morning.

transitivity: both — transitive (the tree *oozes* sap), intransitive (mud *oozed* over the walk)
gloss: To flow out slowly and thickly.
examples: Sap *oozes* from the cut branches every spring.
Mud *oozed* across the sidewalk after the slide.
Lava was still *oozing* from the fissure a month later.

transitivity: both — transitive (the roof *drips* water), intransitive (the faucet *dripped*)
gloss: To fall or let fall in drops.
examples: Melting snow *drips* off the eaves all afternoon.
Rain *dripped* through the roof into a bucket.
Her coat was *dripping* by the time she got inside.
contrast: One vowel plus one final consonant, so the p doubles: *dripped*, *dripping*.

transitivity: both — transitive (the whale *spouts* water), intransitive (the geyser *spouted*)
gloss: To send out a strong narrow stream of liquid or steam.
examples: The geyser *spouts* every ninety minutes or so.
A whale *spouted* twice off the bow.
Water was *spouting* out of a crack in the old pipe.

gloss: To fall in large amounts, the way water falls over rocks.
examples: Meltwater *cascades* down the rock face every spring.
Rain *cascaded* off the awning in sheets.
Snow was *cascading* off the roof in big wet slabs.

transitivity: both — transitive (the wind *churned* the lake), intransitive (the sea *churned*)
gloss: To move water or another liquid around violently.
examples: The sea *churns* for days after a storm like that.
The wind *churned* the lake into whitecaps.
Gray water was *churning* under the bridge.

gloss: To produce a mass of small white bubbles.
examples: The surf *foams* white all along the point.
The river *foamed* over the rocks below the dam.
The waves came in loud and *foaming*.

transitivity: both — transitive (waves *lapped* the dock), intransitive (water *lapped* at our feet)
gloss: To wash gently against something in small waves.
examples: Small waves *lap* against the dock all night.
The lake *lapped* at the top of the seawall.
The dog was *lapping* water out of a puddle.
contrast: One vowel plus one final consonant, so the p doubles: *lapped*, *lapping*. Often used with *at* or *against*.

transitivity: both — transitive (they *pooled* the runoff), intransitive (rain *pooled* in the yard)
gloss: To collect in one low place instead of draining away.
examples: Rain *pools* in the low corner of the yard every spring.
Water *pooled* on the flat roof and started coming through.
Meltwater was *pooling* around the storm drain.

ru: извиваться, петлять (о реке); брести без цели
gloss: To follow a long winding course instead of a straight one.
examples: The creek *meanders* across the whole valley floor.
The trail *meandered* along the riverbank for a mile.
We spent the afternoon *meandering* through the woods.

ru: направлять (по руслу), отводить; пускать по каналу
gloss: To send water or another flow along a particular path.
examples: These ditches *channel* runoff away from the houses.
The town *channeled* the creek into a concrete culvert back in the 1950s.
Storm drains were *channeling* the water straight into the river.
contrast: American English keeps one l: *channeled*, *channeling*; British English writes *channelled*.

gloss: To form bubbles, or to rise through liquid as bubbles.
examples: Gas *bubbles* through the mud pots all day long.
The spring *bubbled* out of the rocks at the base of the cliff.
Mud was *bubbling* and steaming near the crater.

transitivity: both — transitive (the soil *percolates* the water), intransitive (rain *percolates* down)
gloss: To pass slowly through something that has small holes in it.
examples: Rain *percolates* through the sand into the aquifer.
The water *percolated* slowly down through the gravel.
Coffee was *percolating* on the camp stove when we woke up.

transitivity: both — transitive (mud *splattered* the truck), intransitive (rain *splattered* on the walk)
gloss: To scatter drops of liquid noisily over a surface.
examples: The first fat drops *splatter* the dusty sidewalk.
Mud *splattered* the whole side of the truck.
Rain was *splattering* against the window by the time we left.
contrast: *splatter* and *spatter* both exist; *splatter* is the more common American form.

gloss: To force people or things out of the place where they belong.
examples: A flood like that can *displace* thousands of people in a day.
The fire *displaced* two hundred families on the east side.
Rising water was *displacing* wildlife all along the river.

gloss: To save someone or something from danger.
examples: Volunteers *rescue* dozens of animals after every flood.
The crew *rescued* six people off the rooftops.
They were still *rescuing* people at midnight.
contrast: The silent final e disappears before *-ing*: *rescuing*, not rescueing.

gloss: To burst out suddenly and violently, the way a volcano does.
examples: That volcano *erupts* every few decades.
Kilauea *erupted* again last spring.
Ash has been drifting east since the crater started *erupting*.

transitivity: both — transitive (the crater *spews* ash), intransitive (smoke *spewed* from the vents)
gloss: To throw out a large amount of gas, liquid, or ash with force.
examples: The crater *spews* ash whenever the pressure builds.
The volcano *spewed* lava for eleven days.
Smoke was *spewing* from vents all over the north slope.

gloss: To shake hard, the way the ground does in an earthquake.
examples: The whole valley *quakes* when a big one hits the fault.
The ground *quaked* for almost a full minute.
We stood in the doorway with the floor *quaking* under us.

gloss: To make a long, low, rolling sound.
examples: Thunder *rumbles* across the lake most summer evenings.
The ground *rumbled* a few seconds before the shaking started.
A storm was *rumbling* somewhere off to the west.

gloss: To shake or shove something suddenly and hard.
examples: An aftershock like that *jolts* the whole building.
A 5.2 quake *jolted* the Bay Area before dawn.
We were *jolted* awake at four in the morning.

transitivity: both — transitive (the quake *ruptured* the line), intransitive (the main *ruptured*)
gloss: To burst or tear open under pressure.
examples: A quake this strong can *rupture* gas lines all over the city.
The fault *ruptured* along nearly thirty miles.
Two water mains have *ruptured* since the shaking stopped.

gloss: To make something start happening, usually something sudden or bad.
examples: Heavy rain *triggers* mudslides on the burn scars every winter.
The quake *triggered* a tsunami warning all up the coast.
Warm rain falling on snow is *triggering* floods statewide.
contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, so the r is not doubled: *triggered*, *triggering*.

transitivity: both — transitive (the mud *fossilized* the leaf), intransitive (bones rarely *fossilize*)
gloss: To turn slowly into rock and be preserved as a fossil.
examples: Only a tiny fraction of bones ever *fossilize*.
The fern *fossilized* in the mud of an ancient lakebed.
The museum has a *fossilized* tree trunk from Arizona.
contrast: American spelling *fossilize*; British English writes *fossilise*.

transitivity: both — transitive (they *weathered* the storm), intransitive (the boards *weathered* gray)
gloss: To come through a hard time without breaking, or to be worn and changed by the open air.
examples: These old barns *weather* every storm that comes through.
The town *weathered* the hurricane with almost no damage.
The fence boards have *weathered* to a soft gray.
contrast: The th is voiced, as in *father*: WETH-ur.

gloss: To cut or scrape a deep groove or hole in a surface.
examples: Glaciers *gouge* deep valleys out of solid rock.
The flood *gouged* a channel right across the field.
Ice was *gouging* the bank on the outside of the bend.

transitivity: both — transitive (the frost *tilted* the posts), intransitive (the earth *tilts* on its axis)
gloss: To lean to one side instead of standing straight, or to make something lean.
examples: The earth *tilts* about twenty-three degrees on its axis, and that is what gives us seasons.
The old fence posts *tilted* a little farther every year as the ground froze and thawed.
The big maple was *tilting* toward the house after the storm.

gloss: To come away from a surface in thin small pieces.
examples: Old paint *flakes* fast in this desert sun.
The dry bark *flaked* under my fingers.
The white crust was *flaking* where the spring had dried up.

transitivity: both — transitive (the moon *orbits* the earth), intransitive (the satellite *orbited* for years)
gloss: To travel in a curved path around a planet, a star, or another body.
examples: The moon *orbits* the earth about once a month.
That satellite *orbited* for eleven years before it burned up.
Two small moons are *orbiting* the planet.
contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, so the t is not doubled: *orbited*, *orbiting*. It takes a direct object with no *around*: *orbits the earth*.

gloss: To turn in a circle around a center point.
examples: The earth *revolves* around the sun once a year.
For centuries people believed the sun *revolved* around the earth.
The whole storm system is *revolving* counterclockwise.
contrast: Takes *around*: *revolve around the sun*.

gloss: To block the light of the sun or moon by passing in front of it.
examples: The moon *eclipses* the sun somewhere on earth about twice a year.
The moon completely *eclipsed* the sun for four minutes.
The shadow was already *eclipsing* the bottom edge of the sun.

ru: убывать (о луне); ослабевать, идти на убыль
gloss: To grow gradually smaller or weaker.
examples: The moon *wanes* for two weeks after it is full.
The storm *waned* as soon as it moved inland.
Daylight is *waning* a little earlier every evening now.
contrast: The opposite of *wax*: the moon *waxes and wanes*.

transitivity: both — transitive (water *refracts* light), intransitive (light *refracts* through the ice)
gloss: To bend light as it passes from one material into another.
examples: Raindrops *refract* sunlight and make a rainbow.
The ice *refracted* the light into thin bands of color.
Hot air near the ground was *refracting* the light over the highway.

gloss: To shine softly because the surface is wet.
examples: Wet pavement *glistens* under the streetlights.
The frost *glistened* on every branch that morning.
The whole field was *glistening* with dew.
contrast: The t is silent, as in *listen* and *fasten*: GLIS-uhn.

gloss: To shine with a faint, unsteady light.
examples: A few stars *glimmer* through the haze on a summer night.
Lights from the town *glimmered* across the water.
Something was *glimmering* at the bottom of the creek.

gloss: To shine with a light that keeps changing in brightness.
examples: Stars *twinkle* because the air above us keeps moving.
The lights of the city *twinkled* far below the pass.
The sky was clear, with every star *twinkling*.

gloss: To shine with a soft, wavering light.
examples: Hot asphalt *shimmers* all through August.
The lake *shimmered* in the late sun.
The air over the desert was *shimmering* by ten in the morning.

gloss: To begin to grow light at the start of the day.
examples: Winter days *dawn* gray and cold in this part of the state.
The morning *dawned* clear after three days of rain.
It was just *dawning* when the boats went out.
contrast: With *on* it means to become clear to someone: *it dawned on me that we were lost*.

transitivity: both — transitive (the rain *fogged* the windshield), intransitive (my glasses *fogged*)
gloss: To cover glass with a thin mist so you cannot see through it.
examples: Cold rain *fogs* the inside of the windshield in about a minute.
My glasses *fogged* the second I stepped outside.
The bathroom mirror was completely *fogged*.
contrast: One vowel plus one final consonant, so the g doubles: *fogged*, *fogging*.

gloss: To cover something completely so that it is hidden.
examples: Fog *shrouds* the bridge most mornings in June.
Smoke *shrouded* the city for a solid week.
The peak was *shrouded* in cloud all day.
contrast: Most often in the passive with *in*: *shrouded in fog*.

gloss: To wrap around something and cover it on every side.
examples: Sea fog *envelops* the whole town by evening.
Smoke *enveloped* the valley within an hour.
The mountain was completely *enveloped* in cloud.
contrast: The verb is *envelop* (in-VEL-uhp); the paper *envelope* is a noun with a final e (EN-vuh-lohp).

gloss: To burn or shine with a strong bright flame or light.
examples: The dry hills *blaze* every September.
The barn *blazed* for an hour before help arrived.
We hiked all day under a *blazing* sun.

gloss: To burn slowly with smoke but without flames.
examples: Peat fires *smolder* underground all winter.
The stumps *smoldered* for days after the rain.
Something was still *smoldering* at the edge of the field.
contrast: American spelling *smolder*; British English writes *smoulder*.

gloss: To burn or shine suddenly brighter for a short time.
examples: Embers *flare* whenever the wind picks up.
The fire *flared* when it reached the pines.
The northern lights were *flaring* green over the lake.

transitivity: both — transitive (lightning *sparked* the fire), intransitive (the wires *sparked*)
gloss: To throw off sparks, or to set something going.
examples: Dry lightning *sparks* most of the fires out here.
A downed line *sparked* the blaze on the ridge.
The wires were *sparking* in the rain.

transitivity: both — transitive (a spark *ignited* the grass), intransitive (dry brush *ignites* fast)
gloss: To catch fire, or to set something on fire.
examples: Dry grass *ignites* almost instantly in this heat.
A spark from the mower *ignited* the whole field.
The gas was *igniting* as fast as it reached the surface.

transitivity: both — transitive (he *kindled* a fire), intransitive (damp wood barely *kindles*)
gloss: To get a fire started, or to start burning.
examples: Damp wood barely *kindles*, no matter what you do.
He *kindled* a small fire with birch bark and dry moss.
We spent an hour *kindling* a fire in the wet wind.

transitivity: both — transitive (the fire *charred* the siding), intransitive (the trunks *charred* but stood)
gloss: To burn something until the outside is black.
examples: A fire that hot *chars* the trunks but leaves the roots alive.
The flames *charred* the north side of the house.
We walked through *charred* stumps for a mile.
contrast: One vowel plus one final consonant, so the r doubles: *charred*, *charring*.

gloss: To burn the surface or the edge of something lightly.
examples: A flare-up like that *singes* everything within ten feet.
The fire *singed* the fence but never crossed it.
The heat was *singeing* the leaves on the nearest trees.
contrast: Keeps the e before *-ing*: *singeing*, to keep it apart from *singing*.

gloss: To make a series of small sharp popping sounds.
examples: Dry pine *crackles* and throws sparks.
Ice *crackled* under our boots all the way down.
The radio was *crackling* with reports from the fire line.

gloss: To put out a fire or a light completely.
examples: Rain alone rarely *extinguishes* a fire this big.
Crews *extinguished* the last hot spots on Sunday.
The fire was finally *extinguished* after nine days.
contrast: Ends in *-sh*, so the third-person form adds *-es*: *extinguishes*.

gloss: To throw a lot of water or other liquid over something, usually to put out a fire.
examples: One tanker load can *douse* a small brush fire.
They *doused* the coals before leaving camp.
The plane was *dousing* the ridge with retardant.
contrast: Rhymes with *house*, not with *doze*: DOWS.

gloss: To keep something dangerous from spreading any further.
examples: Crews *contain* most brush fires within a day or two.
They *contained* the spill before it reached the creek.
The fire is sixty percent *contained* tonight.

gloss: To cover something completely and swallow it up.
examples: A fire like that can *engulf* a house in minutes.
Flames *engulfed* the second floor before the trucks arrived.
The wave was *engulfing* the whole beach road.

gloss: To damage a place severely over a wide area.
examples: Wildfires *ravage* the same canyons every few years.
The hurricane *ravaged* the island's farms.
Drought has *ravaged* the whole southern half of the state.

gloss: To destroy a building or a town so completely that nothing is left standing.
examples: A fire that size can *raze* a neighborhood overnight.
The tornado *razed* four blocks on the east side of town.
Half the village had been *razed* by the time the rain came.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *raise* but means the opposite: to flatten something.

gloss: To cover something thickly so that it cannot breathe or burn.
examples: Wet leaves *smother* the grass over the winter.
Ash *smothered* every field within ten miles of the crater.
He was *smothering* the flames with a wet blanket.
contrast: The th is voiced, as in *mother*: SMUTH-ur.

gloss: To send out gas, heat, light, or sound.
examples: The vents *emit* steam day and night.
The fires *emitted* more carbon that summer than the state's cars did all year.
The crater has been *emitting* sulfur gas for months.
contrast: Stress falls on the second syllable, so the t doubles: *emitted*, *emitting*.

transitivity: both — transitive (the roof *vents* hot air), intransitive (gas *vented* from the fissure)
gloss: To let gas, steam, or heat escape through an opening.
examples: The mountain *vents* steam from a dozen cracks.
Gas *vented* from the fissure for two days.
Hot air was *venting* through the roof of the greenhouse.

gloss: To make a deep loud sound that carries a long way.
examples: Thunder *booms* over the canyon and echoes for a long time.
The blast *boomed* across the whole lake.
Thunder was *booming* every few seconds by then.

transitivity: both — transitive (bacteria *decompose* the leaves), intransitive (the log *decomposed*)
gloss: To break down slowly into simpler natural matter.
examples: Leaves *decompose* much faster in warm, wet weather.
The log *decomposed* into soft, dark soil.
Everything in the pile is slowly *decomposing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (the heat *shriveled* the leaves), intransitive (the corn *shriveled*)
gloss: To dry up and become wrinkled and much smaller.
examples: Corn *shrivels* fast in a drought like this one.
The tomatoes *shriveled* right on the vine.
The leaves were already *shriveling* by the middle of July.
contrast: American English keeps one l: *shriveled*, *shriveling*; British English writes *shrivelled*.

transitivity: both — transitive (the waves *disintegrated* the dock), intransitive (the ice *disintegrated*)
gloss: To break apart into small pieces and stop being whole.
examples: Cheap plastic *disintegrates* after a year in this sun.
The old dock *disintegrated* in the first big storm.
The ice shelf is *disintegrating* along its whole edge.

transitivity: both — transitive (salt air *oxidizes* the metal), intransitive (iron *oxidizes* fast)
gloss: To combine with oxygen, the way iron does when it rusts.
examples: Iron *oxidizes* quickly in salt air.
The copper roof *oxidized* to a pale green.
The cut apple was already *oxidizing* on the counter.
contrast: American spelling *oxidize*; British English writes *oxidise*.

gloss: To die because of harsh conditions or a disaster.
examples: Seedlings *perish* if the frost comes early.
Thousands of fish *perished* when the lake warmed.
Whole herds have *perished* in this drought.

transitivity: both — transitive (fire *regenerates* the grassland), intransitive (the forest *regenerated*)
gloss: To grow back after being damaged or destroyed.
examples: Some pines only *regenerate* after a fire.
The forest *regenerated* faster than anyone expected.
The reef is slowly *regenerating* where the water stayed cool.

gloss: To give something what it needs to live and grow.
examples: Floods *nourish* the soil all along the delta.
Winter rain *nourished* the grass right through spring.
The river has been *nourishing* these fields for centuries.

gloss: To be completely full of living things that are moving around.
examples: The marsh *teems* with birds in April.
The bay once *teemed* with salmon.
The pond was *teeming* with tadpoles by May.
contrast: Takes *with*: *teeming with fish*. Sounds exactly like *team*.

gloss: To hold something in and keep it from escaping or being lost.
examples: Sandy soil does not *retain* water very well.
The concrete *retained* heat long past sundown.
Clouds are *retaining* enough heat tonight to keep the frost off.

gloss: To keep someone or something safe from harm.
examples: The dunes *protect* the houses behind them from the surf.
Sandbags *protected* the shop from two feet of water.
These wetlands have been *protected* since 1974.
contrast: Takes *from* or *against*: *protect the pipes from freezing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (mud *caked* the wheels), intransitive (wet ash *cakes* and hardens)
gloss: To cover something in a thick layer that dries hard.
examples: Wet ash *cakes* on everything and dries like cement.
Mud *caked* the wheels until they barely turned.
Our boots were *caked* with red clay.

transitivity: both — transitive (the wind *parted* the fog), intransitive (the clouds *parted*)
gloss: To move apart and leave an opening in the middle.
examples: The clouds *part* for an hour most afternoons.
The fog *parted* just long enough for us to see the island.
A strip of blue showed where the clouds were *parting*.
